links.note: The three genuine options are exactly the grouping bases the chapter used - appearance, feel, solubility - which 32727 lists in order; conductivity is outside the chapter. 32717 teaches that classification needs a property but names no set.
The grocer keeping spices in one corner and pulses in another is 32718's own closing example of classification already surrounding the reader.
Metals losing lustre to air and moisture, so that lustre shows on a freshly cut surface - stated in 32719.
Guna as the twenty properties of matter in the Ayurvedic list - 32726. (The stem's word is OCR-mangled from Ayurveda.)
A container material must be able to hold water - the constraint Activity 6.3 sets in 32718, run against a porous option.
Slips as protective or decorative coats in multiple colours - 32716's pottery note.
The definition of a material - any substance used to create an object - 32715.
Classification defined as arranging objects into groups - 32717.
Iron, copper, zinc, aluminium and gold are named as metals in 32719, where lustre is tied to metals.
Non-lustrous materials - paper, wood, rubber, jute - 32719.
Soft defined by easy compression or scratching - 32720.
Transparent defined in the hide-and-seek section, 32721.
Mass and volume as the pair every material shares, which is how 32725 defines matter.
Materials as types of matter used to make objects - the closing relation stated in 32725.
